inputs.need:
I am a nurse researcher in the supportive care service of a regional cancer centre that starts systemic treatment for about 1,900 adults a year. Our oncologists and social workers keep hearing about patients who delay treatment, miss appointments or cannot afford parking, travel and medicines, but the centre has no routine way to find these patients. We want to know how common financial toxicity is among our patients receiving systemic treatment, which groups are most affected, and whether the question about money in our existing distress screening finds the people who need help.

My plan is a cross-sectional survey of adults receiving chemotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted therapy at the centre over three months, using a validated 11-item financial toxicity questionnaire together with questions about income, employment, travel distance, benefits and out-of-pocket spending. We would also compare each respondent's answer to the financial problems checkbox on the distress screening form with their questionnaire score.

The centre's patient and family advisory council supports the work, and the research ethics board approved the protocol this month. We have a research coordinator two days a week and can offer the questionnaire on paper, on a tablet or by telephone, in English and three other languages, with interpreters paid from the supportive care budget. I need help with sampling (consecutive patients or a random sample of clinic days), the sample size for comparing groups, how to reduce non-response among the patients most affected, and how to report results so that the centre can decide whether to set up a financial navigation service.

records.title: Prevalence of financial toxicity among adults receiving systemic cancer therapy: a five-centre survey with a validated 11-item questionnaire
records.authors: Mensah-Kowalski A, Lindqvist-Obi J, Carvalho-Stroud E
records.abstract: We surveyed 1,450 adults receiving systemic therapy in five cancer centres with a validated financial toxicity questionnaire; 64 percent of those approached responded. Thirty-eight percent reported moderate or severe financial toxicity. Financial toxicity was more common among patients under 65, those with household income in the lowest two quintiles, those who had stopped working because of treatment and those living more than 50 kilometres from the centre. Patients receiving oral targeted therapy reported higher out-of-pocket spending on medicines. Non-respondents were younger and more often lived far from the centre, so the prevalence may be underestimated.

records.title: Out-of-pocket costs and travel burden during chemotherapy: a patient diary study
records.abstract: Two hundred and twelve patients receiving chemotherapy kept a spending diary for twelve weeks. Travel and parking made up 41 percent of out-of-pocket spending, medicines and supplements 27 percent and lost income of family carers was reported by a third of patients. Patients living in rural areas spent on average twice as much on travel as those living in the city. Spending was highest in the first six weeks of treatment. The authors note that diary completion fell over time, especially among patients who were most unwell.

records.title: Agreement between a single financial distress item and a multi-item financial toxicity score in oncology outpatients
records.authors: Brennan-Oyelowo S, Haddad-Lund P, Tanaka-Achebe V
records.abstract: In 640 oncology outpatients we compared a single financial problems item from a distress screening checklist with a validated multi-item financial toxicity score. The single item identified 61 percent of patients with moderate or severe financial toxicity on the multi-item score, and agreement beyond chance was moderate (kappa 0.45). Patients who did not tick the item despite high scores were more often older and more often described money as a private matter. The authors suggest that a single checkbox can support but not replace a short validated measure.

records.title: Non-response in cancer patient surveys: who is missed and does it matter?
records.abstract: Across four surveys of cancer patients, non-respondents were younger, had lower incomes and more often spoke a language other than the survey language. Offering the questionnaire in several modes (paper, tablet and telephone) and in the main community languages raised response from 48 to 66 percent and reduced the difference in response between income groups by half. Estimates of unmet need changed by up to eight percentage points when weighting for non-response. The authors recommend recording the characteristics of everyone approached so that non-response can be described and weighted.

records.title: Financial toxicity and skipped or delayed cancer treatment: a systematic review of 19 observational studies
records.abstract: We included 19 observational studies examining financial toxicity and adherence to cancer treatment. Across studies, patients with financial toxicity more often skipped doses, delayed treatment or missed appointments (pooled odds ratio 1.8, 95 percent CI 1.4 to 2.3), with substantial heterogeneity. Most studies were cross-sectional, so the direction of the association is uncertain, and adherence was usually self-reported. No study tested whether screening followed by financial navigation improved adherence. The authors call for routine measurement of financial toxicity with a validated instrument.

records.title: Financial navigation in cancer centres: a before-after evaluation of a navigator service
records.abstract: One cancer centre introduced a financial navigator who helped patients with benefits, travel grants and medicine costs. Among 310 patients who used the service, median out-of-pocket spending over three months fell by 38 percent and the mean financial toxicity score improved modestly. Patients referred through distress screening were less likely to be the most affected than those referred by social workers. The navigator saw a median of three patients a day, and waiting times for a first appointment rose to three weeks by the end of the year. The evaluation had no comparison group and patients chose whether to use the service.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A multicentre survey found moderate or severe financial toxicity in 38 percent of adults on systemic therapy, concentrated among younger, lower-income, not working and distant patients, probably underestimated by non-response. Travel and parking dominate out-of-pocket spending. A single distress-screening item misses about four in ten affected patients. Multi-mode, multilingual administration substantially reduces non-response bias. Financial toxicity is associated with poorer adherence, and a navigator service lowered spending without a comparison group.
response.gradeRationale: Consistent survey evidence with validated measures and a measurement study for the prevalence and screening questions; adherence and navigation evidence is weaker. Moderate certainty for prevalence and screening agreement.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; five claims recorded; overall certainty moderate.

steps.note: Appraisal of six retrieved records on the production scan path (S13); certainty moderate over inspected records.

response.title: Financial toxicity among adults in their first six months of systemic cancer therapy: a cross-sectional survey
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the prevalence of moderate or severe financial toxicity by group and the agreement of a distress screening checkbox with a validated questionnaire. Design: cross-sectional survey in four day units from February to April 2027, offered in three modes and four languages, with non-response weighting. Results and conclusions will be written after the survey.
response.introduction: Financial toxicity is common during systemic cancer therapy and associated with delayed or skipped treatment, but screening often relies on a single item.
response.methods: Clinic days were sampled at random and every eligible patient approached. The primary outcome was a moderate or severe score on a validated questionnaire; the checkbox closest in time was linked for the agreement analysis.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present response by group, weighted prevalence, prevalence ratios, checkbox agreement and spending.
response.discussion: The discussion will size a navigation service and state whether the checkbox is adequate for screening.
response.limitations: Patients who stopped treatment are missed; self-report; one centre.
response.conclusion: To be written after the survey; it will not claim effects of navigation.
response.summary: STROBE-structured draft with results left empty.
